blocks.text: Writing an MCP server with the low level SDK means dealing with JSON-RPC handlers, manually shaped schemas, and a fair amount of boilerplate before you write any real logic.
FastMCP removes almost all of that. You write an ordinary function, add one decorator, and the framework figures out the rest.
It exists for both Python and TypeScript, and it has become the most common way people actually build MCP servers day to day.
1. What FastMCP Actually Is

blocks.alt: A decorated function becomes a registered MCP tool

blocks.text: FastMCP is a higher level framework built on top of the official MCP SDKs, in both Python and TypeScript.
It does not replace the protocol or invent new concepts, it just gives you a much shorter path to the same server.
Tools, resources, and prompts still mean exactly what they mean in the base protocol.
2. Why It Exists
The low level SDK is explicit by design, every schema field, every handler registration is spelled out by hand.
That explicitness is useful when you need fine control, but it slows down the common case of exposing a simple function.
FastMCP was built to remove that friction, so a working tool takes a few lines instead of dozens.
3. Installing FastMCP
The Python package installs like any other, and gives you a ready made server object to import.

code.content:
pip install fastmcp

# project layout
my-server/
  server.py
  requirements.txt

blocks.text: The TypeScript version follows the same shape, installed as a single npm dependency.
4. Creating a Server Instance

blocks.alt: A single line creates a FastMCP server instance ready for tools

blocks.text: Every FastMCP server starts with a single object, given a name that identifies it to whatever host connects.

code.content:
from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("notes-server")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

blocks.text: That is already a complete, if empty, MCP server, ready to accept a connection over stdio.
5. The at mcp.tool Decorator

blocks.alt: The tool decorator wraps a plain function into a callable tool

blocks.text: This is the core idea of FastMCP. You write a normal function, add one decorator above it, and it becomes a callable MCP tool.
No manual schema, no handler registration call, no separate description object.
6. Automatic Schema Generation From Type Hints

blocks.alt: Type hints on a function automatically generate its schema

blocks.text: The JSON Schema a client sees is built entirely from the function signature, no separate schema file or dict to keep in sync.
A plain string hint becomes a string field, an int becomes a number field, and a default value becomes an optional field.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Python type hint","Generated schema field"],"rows":[["str","string"],["int","integer"],["float","number"],["bool","boolean"],["list[str]","array of string"],["str = \"default\"","string, not required"]]}

blocks.text: The docstring becomes the tool description, so writing a clear docstring is not optional documentation, it is part of the schema.
7. Pydantic Models for Richer Input
When a tool needs a nested or more structured input, a Pydantic model works as the parameter type and FastMCP expands it into a nested schema automatically.
Field level validation, like the priority range above, carries straight through to the generated schema.
8. Registering Resources the Fast Way
Resources get the same decorator treatment, a URI string passed to the decorator and a function that returns the content.
9. Resource Templates
A curly brace placeholder in the URI becomes a function parameter, matching the pattern from the low level SDK.
10. Registering Prompts
Prompts use the same idea again, a decorator over a function that returns text or a list of messages.
11. The Context Object

blocks.alt: A context object gives a tool access to logging and progress reporting

blocks.text: A tool that needs to report progress or log messages can accept a Context parameter, and FastMCP injects it automatically.

code.content:
from fastmcp import Context

@mcp.tool()
async def reindex_notes(ctx: Context) -> str:
    """Rebuild the search index, reporting progress along the way."""
    all_notes = load_notes()
    for i, n in enumerate(all_notes):
        index_note(n)
        await ctx.report_progress(i + 1, len(all_notes))
    return f"Indexed {len(all_notes)} notes"

blocks.text: You never construct the Context yourself, FastMCP recognizes the type hint and fills it in for you.
12. Async and Sync Functions Both Work
A tool function can be defined with def or async def, FastMCP handles both without any extra configuration.
Reach for async def whenever the function calls a database, an API, or anything else that waits on IO.
13. Error Handling
Raising a normal exception inside a tool function is enough, FastMCP catches it and reports it back as a tool error automatically.
There is no need to build a custom error response shape by hand, the framework converts the exception for you.
14. Running and Choosing a Transport
Calling run() defaults to stdio, the common choice for a locally spawned server.
15. FastMCP Compared to the Low Level SDK

blocks.alt: FastMCP is compared against the low level SDK

blocks.text: FastMCP is not a competing protocol implementation, it is a thin, ergonomic layer over the same low level SDK.
Everything the low level SDK does, JSON-RPC handling, capability negotiation, transport management, still happens underneath.

blocks.title: When to drop to the low level SDK
blocks.content: Reach for the low level SDK directly only when you need protocol behavior FastMCP does not expose, most servers never hit that wall.

blocks.text: 16. The TypeScript Side of FastMCP
The TypeScript version mirrors the same idea, a decorator style registration and a Zod schema instead of type hints.

Common Mistakes

items: Skipping type hints entirely, which leaves FastMCP with nothing to build a useful schema from.
Leaving out the docstring, so the tool ships with a missing or unhelpful description.
Assuming FastMCP hides the protocol completely, when in fact the low level SDK is still doing the real work underneath.
Blocking on a heavy synchronous call inside an async def tool instead of awaiting it properly.
Reaching for a raw dict instead of a Pydantic model when the input actually has real structure.
Forgetting that FastMCP exists for TypeScript too, and rewriting a working Python server in the low level SDK just to reach Node.

blocks.text: Practice
Write a FastMCP tool called convert_temp that takes a value and a unit, and returns the converted temperature.
Key Takeaway
FastMCP gives you the full MCP protocol with almost none of the manual setup, a decorator and a type hinted function are usually enough.
It sits on top of the same low level SDK, so nothing about the protocol changes, only how much code you have to write to reach it.
